learning: Track width at y 0.08 is monotone so far (0.10: 496.4, 0.12: 561.6). Yaw per PWM count falls as the track widens, so 0.14 tests whether the bend overshoot found at 0.10 reverses. Slalom has been 0 of 20 at every geometry tested, so it is not the target of this race.
notes: Complete robot for the wheel_track 0.14 test at y 0.08. The controller is unchanged from iteration 5 so that only track width differs. The race is compared against iteration 5 (561.6) and iteration 6 (496.4).
rationale: Iteration 5 (wheel_track 0.12, y 0.08, score 561.6) is the best design. Iteration 6 tested wheel_track 0.10 and scored 496.4: s-bend off-track exits rose from 9 to 15 of 20, max_error rose from 0.047 to 0.057, and control_effort rose from 12.2 to 12.5. That makes the score move monotonically with track width at y 0.08 (0.10 gives 496.4, 0.12 gives 561.6), and the narrower direction is the wrong one. The Builder's candidate tests the other direction, wheel_track 0.14. I accept that test, because the contract's turn-rate equation (wheel speed difference divided by wheel_track) means a wider track gives less yaw per PWM count and should reduce overshoot in bends. This is an extrapolation from two points, so I treat it as a test rather than a settled result. I keep the controller identical to iteration 5 (kp 4.0, ki 0.1, kd 0.5, base_speed 1.6, last_direction, weights [2,1,0,-1,-2]). Raising kp to offset the roughly 14 percent smaller yaw per command would confound the one-variable test, and the 0.10 result showed that changing yaw gain without evidence hurts. Sensors stay at y 0.08, 16 mm footprints and x = ±0.024, 0.012, 0. Expected: s-bend off-track exits below 9 of 20, lower control_effort, oval finish near 1.0, oscillation below about 0.4. Risk: a sluggish response on the bends would show up as higher max_error; if that happens, revert to wheel_track 0.12.
